q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: In 1807, it became illegal to trade slaves in British ships or from British ports, and in 1833 the Emancipation Act abolished slavery throughout the British Empire.
o: The Emancipation Act of 1833 abolished slavery throughout the British Empire
The Emancipation Act of 1807 abolished slavery throughout the British Empire

q.t: Who set up the first formal anti-slavery groups in Britain?
q.e: There were people in Britain who opposed the slave trade. The first formal anti-slavery groups were set up by the Quakers in the late 1700s, and they petitioned Parliament to ban the practice.

q.t: Who was William Wilberforce?
q.e: William Wilberforce, an evangelical Christian and a member of Parliament, played an important part in changing the law. Along with other abolitionists, he succeeded in turning public opinion against the slave trade.
o: An evangelical Christian and MP who helped turn opinion against the slave trade
A Quaker who founded the first anti-slavery group
The admiral who commanded the fleet at Trafalgar
The first Prime Minister of Great Britain

q.t: What did the American colonists mean by 'no taxation without representation'?
q.e: The British government wanted to tax the colonies. The colonists saw this as an attack on their freedom and said there should be 'no taxation without representation' in the British Parliament.
o: They should not be taxed without representation in the British Parliament
They should not pay taxes to their own colonial assemblies
Taxes should be collected by the Royal Navy

q.t: In which year did Britain recognise the independence of the American colonies?
q.e: In 1776, 13 American colonies declared their independence, stating that people had a right to establish their own governments. The colonists eventually defeated the British army and Britain recognised the colonies' independence in 1783.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: Britain's navy fought against combined French and Spanish fleets, winning the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805. Admiral Nelson was in charge of the British fleet at Trafalgar and was killed in the battle. In 1815, the French Wars ended with the defeat of Napoleon by the Duke of Wellington at the Battle of Waterloo.
o: Nelson commanded at Trafalgar and Wellington at Waterloo
Wellington commanded at Trafalgar and Nelson at Waterloo

q.t: Where can Admiral Nelson's ship, HMS Victory, be visited?
q.e: Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square, London, is a monument to him. His ship, HMS Victory, can be visited in Portsmouth.

q.t: By what nickname was the Duke of Wellington known?
q.e: In 1815, the French Wars ended with the defeat of the Emperor Napoleon by the Duke of Wellington at the Battle of Waterloo. Wellington was known as the Iron Duke and later became Prime Minister.

q.t: Which TWO crosses, besides the cross of St George, make up the Union Flag?
q.e: The Union Flag consists of three crosses: the cross of St George, patron saint of England, a red cross on a white ground; the cross of St Andrew, patron saint of Scotland, a diagonal white cross on a blue ground; and the cross of St Patrick, patron saint of Ireland, a diagonal red cross on a white ground.

q.t: Why does the Welsh dragon not appear on the Union Flag?
q.e: The Welsh dragon does not appear on the Union Flag because, when the first Union Flag was created in 1606 from the flags of Scotland and England, the Principality of Wales was already united with England.
o: Wales was already united with England when the first Union Flag was created
Wales had its own separate parliament at the time
The dragon was thought to be unlucky
Wales did not have a flag until the 19th century

q.t: How old was Queen Victoria when she became queen, and for roughly how long did she reign?
q.e: In 1837, Queen Victoria became queen of the UK at the age of 18. She reigned until 1901, almost 64 years. Her reign is known as the Victorian Age.

q.t: What was the estimated population of the British Empire at its height in the Victorian period?
q.e: During the Victorian period, the British Empire grew to cover all of India, Australia and large parts of Africa. It became the largest empire the world has ever seen, with an estimated population of more than 400 million people.

q.t: What did the repealing of the Corn Laws in 1846 do?
q.e: The government began to promote policies of free trade, abolishing a number of taxes on imported goods. One example of this was the repealing of the Corn Laws in 1846. These had prevented the import of cheap grain.
o: It allowed cheap grain to be imported
It banned the export of British wool
It introduced a tax on imported cotton
It limited factory hours for women and children

q.t: In 1847, what limit was placed by law on the working hours of women and children?
q.e: Working conditions in factories gradually became better. In 1847, the number of hours that women and children could work was limited by law to 10 hours per day.

q.t: Which TWO engineers pioneered the railway engine just before Victoria came to the throne?
q.e: Just before Victoria came to the throne, the father and son George and Robert Stephenson pioneered the railway engine and a major expansion of the railways took place in the Victorian period.

q.t: Which railway did Isambard Kingdom Brunel construct?
q.e: Brunel was an engineer who built tunnels, bridges, railway lines and ships. He was responsible for constructing the Great Western Railway, which was the first major railway built in Britain. It runs from Paddington Station in London to the south west of England, the West Midlands and Wales.

q.t: Where was the Great Exhibition of 1851 held?
q.e: In 1851, the Great Exhibition opened in Hyde Park in the Crystal Palace, a huge building made of steel and glass. Exhibits ranged from huge machines to handmade goods.
o: In the Crystal Palace, in Hyde Park

q.t: Which medal did Queen Victoria introduce during the Crimean War?
q.e: From 1853 to 1856, Britain fought with Turkey and France against Russia in the Crimean War. Queen Victoria introduced the Victoria Cross medal during this war. It honours acts of valour by soldiers.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
Florence Nightingale was born in Italy to English parents.
q.e: Florence Nightingale was born in Italy to English parents. At the age of 31, she trained as a nurse in Germany. In 1854, she went to Turkey and worked in military hospitals, treating soldiers who were fighting in the Crimean War.

q.t: Where did Florence Nightingale establish her training school for nurses?
q.e: In 1860 she established the Nightingale Training School for nurses at St Thomas' Hospital in London. The school was the first of its kind and still exists today. She is often regarded as the founder of modern nursing.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: The Irish Nationalist movement had grown strongly through the 19th century. Some, such as the Fenians, favoured complete independence. Others, such as Charles Stuart Parnell, advocated 'Home Rule', in which Ireland would remain in the UK but have its own parliament.
o: The Fenians favoured complete independence for Ireland
The Fenians favoured Home Rule within the UK

q.t: What did the Reform Act of 1832 abolish?
q.e: The Reform Act of 1832 had greatly increased the number of people with the right to vote. The Act also abolished the old pocket and rotten boroughs and more parliamentary seats were given to the towns and cities.
o: The old pocket and rotten boroughs

q.t: Which TWO changes did the Chartists demand, according to the handbook?
q.e: In the 1830s and 1840s, a group called the Chartists campaigned for reform. They wanted six changes: for every man to have the vote, elections every year, for all regions to be equal in the electoral system, secret ballots, for any man to be able to stand as an MP, and for MPs to be paid.
o: The abolition of the House of Lords

q.t: Emmeline Pankhurst helped found which group in 1903?
q.e: Emmeline Pankhurst set up the Women's Franchise League in 1889. In 1903 she helped found the Women's Social and Political Union (WSPU). This was the first group whose members were called 'suffragettes'.
o: The Women's Social and Political Union
